summary: Provides a generic information model and format for authorization information, saying which entities may do what operations on which resources. It is useful for Internet of Things systems with many entities, and gives two variants of a specific instantiation for REST resources. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A simple permission list that says who can do what with which thing.

questions: what is the authorization information format
aif cbor vs json media type
subtitle: A compact allow-list format that tells a constrained device which resources a client may use and how.

tldr.problem: Constrained Internet of Things devices must decide which requests are authorized, and an authorization manager needs a compact way to hand them detailed permissions.
tldr.mechanism: The Authorization Information Format (AIF) is a list of pairs of an object identifier and a permission set. The REST-specific form uses URI paths and a bit set of CoAP methods, with optional Dynamic-X permissions for resources created later.
tldr.outcome: AIF has JSON and CBOR encodings with registered media types and CoAP Content-Formats. It is a Proposed Standard and relies on surrounding cryptographic armor to name the subject.

today: RFC 9237 is a Proposed Standard, published in August 2022. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Compact Authorization Format
sections.content:
Constrained devices in the Internet of Things must decide which requested operations are authorized, check that the authorization applies to the authenticated requester, and check that the devices they call are the intended ones. To move detailed authorization information from an authorization manager, such as an ACE-OAuth authorization server (RFC 9200), to a device, a compact format is needed.

This RFC defines the Authorization Information Format (AIF), both as a general structure and as a specific form for REST resources and the permissions on them. CoAP (RFC 7252) is used for the examples, and data shapes are written in CDDL.
sections.eli5: Small gadgets need to know what visitors are allowed to do, and they cannot read long, fancy documents. So this is a very short permission list.

sections.title: The Information Model
sections.content:
The semantics are those of an allow-list: everything is denied until explicitly allowed. The underlying model is an access matrix with permissions for each subject and object pair. An AIF data item is a single row of that matrix, sometimes called a capability list, so AIF MUST be used in a way that unambiguously identifies the subject, for example in the armor around it.

The generic form is a list of pairs of an object identifier (type Toid) and permissions (type Tperm). In CDDL: AIF-Generic<Toid, Tperm> = [* [Toid, Tperm]]. A common specific shape uses a text string for Toid and an unsigned number acting as a bit set for Tperm.
sections.eli5: Imagine a chart of every person and every room. AIF is just one person's row of the chart: a list of rooms and what that person may do in each.

sections.title: The REST-Specific Model
sections.content:
For REST resources, the object identifier is the URI of a resource on a CoAP server. The server part of the URI is authenticated during access, so AIF covers only the path and query (the URI-local-part). AIF MUST be used so that it is clear which target enforces the authorizations. Permissions are the subset of REST (CoAP or HTTP) methods that are allowed.

The RFC's example: a device offers /s/temp with GET, /a/led with PUT and GET, and /dtls with POST.

The simple model has limits. It only grants access to statically identifiable objects and does not support URI templates, it cannot express conditions such as “opening a door is allowed if it is not locked”, and it has no special access to resources the subject created itself.
sections.eli5: The list names web-style addresses on the device, like a temperature sensor you may read and a lamp you may read and change.

sections.title: Dynamic Resource Creation
sections.content:
The extended model gives defined access to resources that the subject itself caused to be created. For a method X, a Dynamic-X permission means the subject may use method X on resources returned in a 2.01 (201 Created) response through a Location-indicating mechanism (Location-* options in CoAP or the Location header in HTTP) to a request the subject made to the listed resource.

In the example, /a/make-coffee has POST, Dynamic-GET and Dynamic-DELETE. A POST might return the location of a new resource on the coffee machine, which the subject can read to see the status and delete to cancel the operation. The extended model is presumed once any Dynamic-X permission appears, so no separate switch is needed.
sections.eli5: You may order a coffee, and you get a ticket. Your permission also covers checking or cancelling that one coffee, but not anyone else's.

sections.title: The Data Model and Encodings
sections.content:
In the data model the object identifier is a text string with the URI-local-part, and the permission set becomes one number, REST-method-set. It is built by merging entries with the same path, converting each non-dynamic method to its CoAP method number minus 1, converting Dynamic-X to the number for X plus a Dynamic-Offset of 32, and taking two to the power of each resulting number, combined with a bitwise OR.

For the example, GET is bit 0, POST bit 1, PUT bit 2, DELETE bit 3, FETCH bit 4, PATCH bit 5 and iPATCH bit 6. The example list becomes the JSON [["/s/temp",1],["/a/led",5],["/dtls",2]] (40 bytes) or the equivalent CBOR (28 bytes). Because the offset is 32, all future registered CoAP methods can be expressed both normally and in Dynamic-X form, but only dynamic forms of methods 1 to 21 are typically usable in JSON.
sections.eli5: Each action has its own light switch. Turning on a few switches makes a single number, which is a tiny way to say what is allowed.

sections.title: Media Types and Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media types application/aif+cbor and application/aif+json. Both have optional parameters Toid and Tperm, with defaults URI-local-part and REST-method-set. A specification wanting different types is expected to register them as parameters in a new IANA subregistry (policy: Specification Required) and register a matching Content-Format.

CoAP Content-Format IDs 290 (application/aif+cbor) and 291 (application/aif+json) were registered.
sections.eli5: Official labels were made for the two ways of writing the list, so devices can tell which one they are holding.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of CoAP apply when AIF is used with it, and those of JSON and CBOR apply to the data formats. A specification that uses AIF must ensure its cryptographic armor meets its goals, unambiguously identifies the subject, and supplies context such as scheme and authority so the full object identity can be derived. It must also choose Toid and Tperm types with enough precision that all parties agree on each pair.

A plain implementation that only knows the basic REST model and receives Dynamic-X permissions needs to either reject the whole data item or act only on the permissions it understands, so the allow-list meaning holds. An implementation of the dynamic model needs to carefully track the dynamically created objects and the subjects to which the permissions apply.
sections.eli5: The list is only safe if you also know exactly who it belongs to. A device that does not understand some entries must ignore them instead of guessing.
